en: The Ritual Manual for the Empowerment of the Great Maṇḍala of the Cakravartin King;
formerly titled *Akāśagarbha*, newly titled *Sarvasādhitaka-śrī*.

The Ritual for Empowerment in the Great Maṇḍala of the Cakravartin King, together with the Forms and Colors of the Vajradhātu Assembly, compiled by the Śramaṇa Śrī of Dongdu Seongseonsa Temple, within the Samaya Realm of the Inner Court, on the central platform of the Path.
Depict the Buddha, the World-Honored One,
seated upon a lion throne adorned with various jewels;
the Noble One’s body sits upon a white lotus flower.
His body is the color of white gold.
He is seated in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*), manifesting the signs of having entered the King of Supreme Samādhis.
Manifesting the appearance of preaching the Dharma,
from his entire body there universally issued twelve golden wheels with blazing light,
encircling him like a wheel.
From the crown of his head, various rays of light—
blue, yellow, red, and white— stream forth,
endowed with the marks of a great hero.
He leaned against the Bodhi tree,
which had various kinds of leaves like *cintāmaṇi* jewels.
Above the tree-shaped [canopy], various silken streamers were tied;
some were adorned with vaiḍūrya jewels, celestial fruits, and exquisite garments,
while others hung down like clouds raining forth.
There were various sprouts,
upon which auspicious birds sat together; or else,
amidst the branches, various jeweled leaves had already formed kalpa-trees.
The Blessed One’s two shoulders rest against the rear of that tree.
Beneath the Buddha’s right seat, one should paint the form of a Wheel-Turning King (cakravartin),
seated upon a white lotus flower.
One should practice the visualization of the Buddha’s majesty:
his body is golden in color,
pervaded by a radiant light.
The seven treasures were fully manifested;
only the wheel-treasure was encircled by light as it rested upon a lotus flower.
The remaining six jewels are placed in order as follows:

in the southeast corner is Cūrṇita-uṣṇīṣa; in the south, Vijaya-uṣṇīṣa; in the southwest corner, Anantasvara-uṣṇīṣa; in the west, Sitātapatrā-uṣṇīṣa; in the northwest corner, Uṣṇīṣaśītala; and in the north, Raśmijvalita-uṣṇīṣa, all seated upon white lotus flowers.
Surrounded by various kinds of light,
he sits amidst a blazing radiance;
his body is golden in color.

Holding a cintāmaṇi jewel in his hand, he is the most excellent Buddha-uṣṇīṣa in the northeast corner. Directly to the east is the High Buddha-uṣṇīṣa, in the form of a great king, seated upon a white lotus flower.
Holding a *kūṣmāṇḍa* fruit in his hand, [the deity] beholds the majesty of the Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin). Above the middle court are the names of the ten Uṣṇīṣas.
Next, in the second court, starting from the northeast corner of the boundary path leading to the solitary ancient vajra, one should draw toward the south.

In the southeast corner is the Bodhisattva Dharmapāramitā; next are the Bodhisattvas Mahāsthāmaprāpta, Avalokiteśvara, Parṇaśavarī, and Tārā, all adorned with various ornaments and wearing light garments.
His body is neither coarse nor slender, but of moderate form;
his right hand holds a blue lotus,
and his left hand is in the mudrā of granting boons (varada-mudrā).
Seated upon a flower pedestal;
he is light green in color. Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva. Vajratārā (Vikrīḍitā) Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva is white in body, with three eyes and four arms.
The upper right hand holds a staff;
the upper left hand holds a flask;
the lower right hand holds a rosary.
The lower left hand holds a lotus flower.
His physical demeanor is tranquil. Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva in White Robes adorns his body with a garland of lotuses and wears a jeweled silk scarf draped across his shoulders.
His right hand holds a cintāmaṇi jewel,
and his left hand is in the gesture of granting boons (varada-mudrā).
He sits upon a lotus flower.
This is the Universal Mother of the Lotus Family, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvararāja, seated upon a precious lotus flower, with palms joined in a gesture of salutation.

In the southwest corner is the Bodhisattva Karma-pāramitā; next is the Bodhisattva Dhyāna-pāramitā, who forms the mudrā of meditative concentration, her body appearing like gold; [then] the Bodhisattva Kṣānti-pāramitā and the Bodhisattva Dāna-pāramitā; and the consort Ākāśa-prabhā, whose form is like that of a goddess.
Seated upon a lotus flower, they assume the posture of joining the palms in salutation.

These are the Bodhisattva Śīlapāramitā, the Bodhisattva Vīryapāramitā, and the Bodhisattva Prajñāpāramitā. In the northwest corner is the Bodhisattva Vajrapāramitā. Next is the body and form of the Bodhisattva Trailokyavijaya-vajra, as described in the Yoga [Tantras]. There are the Vajrapāṇi consort and the Vajrapāṇi youth; their specific forms are not depicted here, as they differ according to their respective names. The Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi holds a white fly-whisk in his right hand.
Holding a vajra in her left hand and seated upon a lotus,
the Vajra Mother Bodhisattva is named Māmakī;
her physical form is like that of a young maiden.
Pale violet-blue in color,
adorned with various kinds of necklaces and ornaments,
he sits upon a lotus flower.
Abiding in the self-nature of Prajñā,
his right hand holds a Brahma-scripture,
and his left hand holds a Cintāmaṇi jewel.
The power of bestowing boons (*vara-dāna-śakti*): one must not have a haughty countenance, but rather a joyful expression.

This is the Vajra-clan Mother. The Bodhisattva Subāhu-kumāra is in the form of a youth; the Bodhisattva Mūrdha-gata-kumāra and the others likewise possess the appearance of having their hair tied up. In the northeast corner is the Bodhisattva Ratna-pāramitā; next is the Bodhisattva Prajñā-pāramitā; the Bodhisattva Maitreya holds a white fly-whisk in his hand; the Bodhisattva Buddhamaitrī and the Bodhisattva Buddhalocanā have forms like those of celestial maidens (*devakanyā*).
Seated upon a precious lotus flower,
adorned with various ornaments,
his body is like the color of gold.
He surveyed the assembled multitude;
he wore a robe of fine silk with its corners draped over his shoulders,
and held a jewel in his right hand.
Her left hand is in the *varada* (boon-granting) mudrā;
she is surrounded by a halo of light, her physical form is serene, and she possesses the marks of a Buddha. Her appearance as a Bodhisattva is like that of a Devī.
The physical appearance is the same as before;
however, the right hand holds a lotus flower,
while the left hand performs the gesture of granting boons (*varada-mudrā*).

The radiance is identical to that described previously and no different. Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva has a golden-colored body; as does the Cintāmaṇi-ratna Bodhisattva. These are the names of the thirty-two holy beings in the second enclosure.
The third courtyard is identical to the second enclosure;

in the southeast corner is the Bodhisattva Gīta-pūjā, whose form and attire are entirely golden. Next are the Bodhisattva Cintāmaṇicakra, the Bodhisattva Citta-utpāda-cakra-pravartana, the Bodhisattva Aṣṭa-mahāsthāna-pratisaṃvid-avalokiteśvara, the Bodhisattva Padma-śrī, and the four-armed Bodhisattva Padma-sundarī.
The right first hand holds a noose;
the left hand holds a battle-axe;
the right second hand performs the gesture of granting boons (*varada-mudrā*).
The second hand on the left holds fruit.
He sits upon a lotus; his radiance is as described before.

[These include] the Bodhisattva Blue-Necked Avalokiteśvara, the Bodhisattva Lotus-Uṣṇīṣa, the Bodhisattva Lotus-Yakṣa, and the Eleven-Faced Avalokiteśvara. In the southwest corner is the Dancing Offering Bodhisattva, whose form and attire are entirely golden. Next is the Nāga King Vālika with seven heads, and the Nāga King Ānanda; these two nāga kings are above.
I have previously seen a Buddha with seven heads, kneeling on the ground with palms joined;
this was Vālika Ānanda, differing only in that he held a flower garland. As for the river goddess Anupama, she is the deity of the Nairañjanā River.
He also saw the Buddha approaching;
his physical marks were like those of the Dragon King Mucilinda, with no other distinguishing features. The Earth-God made offerings to him;
his body was white in color, and he held a precious flower basket with both hands.

With both knees kneeling upon the ground are the Bodhisattva Aparājita and the consort Aparājitā; the Naga King Anavatapta holds a lotus garland and bows with palms joined; and the Naga King Mucilinda, along with the two aforementioned Naga Kings, are blue-black in color.
Like a female form,
with seven heads joined in palms-pressed reverence,
she makes the gesture of prostration.

The front and back are identical. The Dragon Girl has a dignified and beautiful appearance. In the northwest corner is the form of the Bodhisattva Hevajra, whose robes and garments are all golden in color. Next are Acala-vajra, Vajragarbha-bodhisattva, Amṛtakuṇḍali-bodhisattva, and Vajrasundarī-bodhisattva; these are the vidyārājñīs (consorts).
Her form is like that of a celestial maiden;
her body is adorned with various kinds of necklaces and ornaments, and she is blue in color.
She holds a lotus flower in her hand.

Seated upon a mountain of jewels are the Bodhisattvas Vajraprīti, Vajramuṣṭi, Abhayadāna, Pañcaśekhara, Vajrasūcī, and Mālādhāra; the latter’s form and attire are entirely golden. Also seated upon a lotus pedestal are the Bodhisattvas Akṣayamati and Dhāraṇīśvara, and the Bodhisattva Māmaki.
She has the form of a woman;
on her head she wears a jeweled crown,
and in her left hand she holds five ancient vajras.
His right hand is in the mudrā of granting boons;
his physical form is upright and majestic, and his halo is blazing and radiant. The Bodhisattva Mahāmaitrī stands in the posture of performing a prostration.
With palms joined, they sit upon lotus pedestals.

Golden-hued and endowed with sublime beauty, the Bodhisattva Śānta possesses the same appearance as Mahāmaitrī; the Bodhisattva Vimalamati possesses the same appearance as Śānta; the Bodhisattva Gaganāmala possesses the same appearance as Vimalamati; [and] the Bodhisattvas Sāgarabuddhi and Sujātamati—these are the names of the forty noble ones of the third court.

The sequence of the deities who perform the activities in the fourth enclosure outside the Vajradhātu: Regarding the outer offerings, starting from the southeast corner, the Bodhisattva of the lamp offering holds a lamp-stand with both hands.
The body and clothing are both red; next is the deity of the Fire Heaven. The King of the Yama Heaven stands at the gate; the Bodhisattva Vajraghaṇṭā has a body and clothing that are both green.

Holding a bell, he resides at the main entrance. Next is Yama, King of the Dead; the Rākṣasa Lord, located in the southwest corner, is a Bodhisattva with a body and garments of yellow hue, holding incense. Next is the Rākṣasa Lord; Vaiśravaṇa, the Heavenly King, is at the gate, appearing as a Bodhisattva with a vajra-hook, his form and garments blue.

The Hook-Bearer (Āṅkuśī) occupies her primary position; next is Vaiśravaṇa. The Lord of Wind is in the northwest corner. The Incense-Offering Bodhisattva is black in color, with two hands holding an incense burner; she is positioned at the Wind Deity. The Water-Deity King is at the entrance. The Vajrapāśa Bodhisattva’s form and attire are both yellow.
Holding a noose, he occupies the position at the gate; he is Varuṇa. Īśāna is in the northeast corner; the Bodhisattva making offerings with flowers sits upon a white lotus.
His garments and complexion are entirely white.
Holding flowers in both hands, this is the posture of making offerings.
Īśāna and Śakra-devendra [are situated] at the corners; the Bodhisattva Vajraśṛṅkhalā stands at the gate, her form and attire both red.
In the central position of the chain-holders is Śakra; [then] Agni, the Lord of Fire. These are the names of the twenty deities of the fourth court above.
From here, in the fifth court of the food-eaters, one should paint at the four corners the five-pronged vajra seals (*mudrā*) with the fierce appearance of Jvālāmukhī.
In the above Ritual for the Great Consecration of the Wheel King of the Maṇḍala,
there are one hundred and twenty-two names of the deities of the upper altar in total.
The Ācārya bestows the consecration upon the disciple.
One should construct a separate maṇḍala beside the great maṇḍala,
facing the presence of the noble assembly.
Using white powder, measure three cubits and draw a lotus flower throughout the center;
upon the central platform, depict a lion throne.
Have the disciple who has received the consecration and whose flower fell [upon that deity] sit upon it;
have one person who understands the ritual procedures [attend to them].
The disciple holds the parasol and the fly-whisk,
chanting auspicious verses in praise continuously and at a slow pace.
He then takes water from the central flask.
Perform the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) one hundred and eight times.

Instruct the disciple to form the *Buddhoṣṇīṣa-mudrā* and place it upon their crown; the remaining details are explained extensively in the ritual for empowerment (*abhiṣeka*). However, it is necessary to blow the conch and strike the drum.
Perform various kinds of music and so forth.
Now, relying on the sūtras, I shall explain the method for painting an image of a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*);
when one is near such a person and possesses the various requisite streams [of conditions], only then may the ritual procedure be performed.
As extensively described in the sūtras, one should prepare a white cotton cloth measuring five cubits or three cubits square to paint the image of the Noble One.
First, Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, composed of the four jewels— starting from the north with gold— should be depicted as emerging from the great ocean.
In the east is white silver;
in the south, lapis lazuli, blue, and green;
in the west, crystal, red, and the color of precious gems; upon these mountains he sits on a white lotus.
His body was the color of white gold;
he sat cross-legged, having entered the supreme king of samādhis.
From all parts of the body, twelve golden wheels flow forth in all directions,
blazing with intense light; above these,
one should paint mountain peaks composed of various jewels.
From the crown of the noble one’s head, various rays of light—
blue, yellow, red, and white— issue forth,
revolving with sovereign ease.
To the right of the Noble One, one should paint the practitioner of recitation,
holding an incense burner and gazing at the face of the Tathāgata.
Below, one should paint a lotus pond; the rest is as described in the sūtra. One should paint two Great Vidyārājas, their characteristics as described later.
The majestic form of the Great Vidyārāja Hayagrīva: [The mantra: *Haya-grīva* (Hayagrīva).
His body is the color of fire;
he has a wrathful form and a nose like that of a monkey.
Adorned with snake ornaments as necklaces,
bracelets on the arms and upper arms, and a lotus garland bound upon the head,
he assumes a posture of gazing intently.
Next is the Wrathful King Aparājita.
His body is white in color;
he has four arms, knitted eyebrows, and a wrathful countenance.
A tiger skin serves as his skirt;
a python serves as his ear-ornaments;
and the Takṣaka Nāga King serves as his waist-band.
The Naga King Tāpasoṅki regards himself as divine;
he wears a cloak with fringed corners draped over his belly,
and his body is somewhat short in stature.
Adorned with a crown of venomous snakes,
biting his lower lip,
his entire body is surrounded by a blazing aura of intense flames.
The upper right hand holds a vajra;
the lower right hand makes the mudrā of threatening.
The upper left hand holds a trident with three prongs.
The left lower hand holds a battle-axe.
He faces forward in the *aṭṭahāsa* (loud laughter) gesture,
with flames of various colors and forms issuing from his mouth.
The face on the right side is in the posture of gazing;
the face on the left side looks downward;
the face on top of the head is in the posture of surveying the great assembly.
He stands upon a precious lotus flower.
The two sages mentioned above are to be painted on both sides outside the gate of the maṇḍala.
Next, one contemplates the five limbs of the principal deity (bimba).

*Ā*, *Vī*, *Rā*, *Hūṃ*, *Khaṃ*. It is also said that these are the "Jewel Measure" (*ratnamāna*) and "Non-empty" (*amogha*). Vairocana resides at the back of the crown; the others are assigned starting from the forehead.

The syllable *A* is so called because it is sustained by the diamond-jewel ground (*vajraratnabhūmi*) and the ground-element of great compassion (*karuṇādhātu*). The syllable *Vi* is so called because it is nourished by the milk-ocean of merit (*guṇakṣīrasamudra*). The syllable *Ra* is so called because it is warmed and nurtured by the torch of samādhi-wisdom (*samādhiprajñāpradīpa*). The syllable *Hūṃ* is so called because it is developed by the wind of wisdom that removes obstacles (*vighnavināśanajñānavāyu*). The syllable *Khaṃ* is so called because its boundless nature is emptiness (*anantaprakṛtiśūnyatā*), which is without obstruction.
Having first laid out the five limbs, the characteristics of yoga are next explained:
The letter A is the color of pure gold;
it universally manifests as a vajra wheel that empowers the lower body; this is called the yoga seat.
The subtle syllable *su* is the light of the moon; it is not within a gathering of mist.
When empowered upon the *śikhā*, it is called the ocean of great compassion.
The syllable *ra* is the first radiance of the sun; its form is red and resides within a triangle.
Empowering the position of the heart, it is called the majesty of the fire of wisdom,
the syllable HŪṂ, and the flame of the kalpa;
empowering the white tuft (ūrṇā) with the wind-circle of dark-blue *añjana*, it is named the power of mastery.
The missing syllable arises from the great emptiness;
through the empowerment that encompasses all forms, it is placed upon the crown of the head. Therefore, he is named the Peerless One (*Asamasama*).
The subsequent five branches are formed by correlating them with earth, water, fire, wind, and space, as well as the mandala.
Visualize the syllable A beneath the seat;
the Vajra-seat is thus perfected,
its appearance like that of refined gold.
This is precisely the meaning of the precepts.
The form of its altar is square;
it is likewise a maṇḍala.
Visualize the subtle syllable at the navel;
it is white in color and consists of the water of loving-kindness and compassion—
this is precisely the state of meditative concentration.
The form of that maṇḍala is circular, and the outer maṇḍala is like the full moon.
One should visualize the syllable RAḤ at the heart;
its form is crimson-red in color.
This is for the purpose of bestowing grace (*anugraha*). Its altar is triangular,
and the outer altar is likewise triangular.
Visualize the syllable HŪṂ between the eyebrows;
its black color represents the unimpeded wind,
which is the very meaning of liberation.
Visualize the altar as being blue in shape like a half-moon;
the characteristics of the outer altar are the same.
Place the syllable *Khaṃ* upon the crown of the head.
By forming the dot of the Great Emptiness (mahāśūnyatā),
this signifies the meaning of the knowledge and vision of liberation (vimukti-jñāna-darśana).
The mandala is like the meaning of the letter itself.
The empty dot has no form or characteristics,
yet it can accomplish all activities;
this is the meaning of *dhāraṇī*.
Oṃ susūkṣma-vajra—this means "subtly fine like a vajra.
This dhāraṇī can cause whatever is visualized to be accomplished. Oṃ tiṣṭha-vajra—this means "immovable like a vajra."
This dhāraṇī enables one to ensure that nothing is lost in what is being contemplated: Oṃ sphara vajra. This is translated as "pervasive like a vajra."

This dhāraṇī enables the object of contemplation to gradually expand until its measure encompasses the entire dharma-realm. Oṃ saṃhara vajra—this is translated as "penetratingly realizing like a vajra."
This dhāraṇī enables the object of contemplation to be gradually abbreviated until it is like the tip of a hair,
abiding at the limit of the white tuft of hair.
Alternatively, one may dwell at the tip of the nose.
Following what the mind desires, the painting is next described,
O Subāhu Kumāra.
The body and retinue of the Honored One have forms like those of youths;
their golden color is according to their names.
One should paint the majestic form of the Honored One with a sense of awe and trembling.
The seven luminaries revolve around it;
the clouds are dense and vast like a desert expanse; this is Ulamutisi.
Those *nākis* and *kinnaras* should each be depicted in their natural forms,
standing upright upon flowers to the side of the *haya-ghrīva* vidyā.
Next, paint the youth Mūrdhaja and his retinue;
the body of the Honored One is golden in color.
With his topknot hanging down,
he holds a vajra in his left hand and rests his right hand on his hip.
Surrounded by eight piśācas,
he is adorned with vajras and possesses vajra-dust.
Vajrapāśa, Vajrakuṭhāra, and Vajrāṭṭahāsa.
Vajrasiddhālaṃkāra, Vajramukuṭa, and Vajrapinākin.
The ritual implements are arranged according to the text.
The above constitutes the complete transcription of the *Uṣṇīṣa-cakra-maṇḍala* ritual.
Completed on the first day. Recorded by Sōrai Shō.
This manual was transcribed with red ink by the Shamon Dōkai of Tōji.
It appears that this ritual was compiled by the Venerable Kōhō;
however, there is some ambiguity regarding whether the characters "Kō" (弘) and "Hō" (𮗿) are used interchangeably.
This was compiled by the disciples of Master Qinglong;
it is particularly worthy of being taken as a model.
